vignette:
Fatima sits at her desk, the fluorescent light humming overhead. She is running her finger down a column of numbers for the fourth time. The digits blur and then sharpen, blur and sharpen, but she forces her eyes to stay on the page. She knows the column balances—she checked it yesterday, and again this morning—but the thought of missing a single error tightens her chest. Her supervisor once told her she is the most meticulous auditor on the team, and Fatima smiled stiffly, because she cannot explain that her thoroughness is not patience. It is fear.

Three years ago, on a Tuesday afternoon, Fatima received a phone call from her cousin in the old city where she grew up. She was at her desk then too, in the same gray cubicle, and she remembers the way her hand shook as she pressed the phone to her ear. The line crackled, and her cousin’s voice was hollow, reciting words that seemed to belong to someone else’s story. Her younger brother, Khalid—the one who stayed behind when she emigrated fifteen years earlier—had been shopping in the market when a bomb hidden inside a vegetable cart detonated. He was not killed instantly, the cousin said. He died in a clinic an hour later. Fatima did not cry. She hung up, opened her spreadsheet, and continued typing until her shift ended.

She flew back for the funeral, and she insisted on seeing his body before the burial. The morgue was cold and smelled of bleach. The attendant pulled back the white sheet, and Fatima saw Khalid’s face—pale, peaceful, a small cut above his eyebrow that she had never noticed when he was alive. That image embedded itself behind her eyelids. She still sees it every night when she closes her eyes, usually at three in the morning, when she wakes gasping from a dream where the bomb is still ticking and she is running, running, always too late.

After the funeral, Fatima returned to her apartment in the Midwest and tried to resume her life. She cancelled her subscription to the Arabic news channel because every report from the region triggered a hot, tightening sensation in her throat. She stopped calling her cousin, not out of anger but because hearing his voice brought back the crackling phone line. She told herself she was moving on.

But moving on, for an auditor, is not possible when every number feels like a clue to a catastrophe she failed to prevent. At work, she triple-checks the smallest line items. If a $3.50 discrepancy appears in a quarterly report, she cannot rest until she traces it to its source. Her colleagues joke that she is obsessive, but Fatima does not laugh. The stakes feel absolute. One mistake, she thinks, and the whole system collapses. This is not professional pride—it is a vigilance she cannot turn off. She once stayed until midnight to verify a single decimal point, and when she finally drove home, she found herself scanning every shadow between streetlights, her foot hovering over the brake.

She has not dated in years. She tells herself she is too old, too set in her ways. But the truth is simpler. She does not trust herself to protect anyone. If she could not save Khalid from a market street two continents away, how could she keep anyone safe in the same city? That guilt sits in her chest like a stone, and some days she presses her palm there while waiting for the elevator, feeling the slow thud of her heart.

Last week, the senior manager asked her to mentor a new junior auditor. The young woman reminded Fatima of herself thirty years ago—eager, precise, unaware that the world could split open on a Tuesday afternoon. Fatima agreed, but she gave the new hire only terse instructions and avoided eye contact. She did not want to attach herself to someone she might fail.

Tonight, as she locks her desk drawer and walks to the parking lot, she notices a sedan idling a few spaces away. The driver is talking on the phone, his face half-lit. Her pulse jumps, and she stops breathing for a moment. It is nothing—just a man waiting for a passenger. But she does not relax until she is inside her locked car, doors locked, engine running, already planning the safest route home.
